correctness.rationale: Johnson–Kollár’s general quasismoothness criterion reduces sharply because every subset containing a weight-one coordinate is automatically handled. At the \(a\)-vertex, the distinguished coordinate can have weight \(a,b,1\), giving exactly divisibility by \(r+d,r,r+d-1\); the \(b\)-vertex gives \(r-d,r,r-d-1\). The two-heavy subset introduces no additional condition once the singleton conditions hold; in the distinguished weight-one case the hypothesis \(r\ge2\) supplies distinct unit coordinates for the injection. The Reid–Tai chart calculation gives the canonical triangle \(0\le d\le r\), \(a\le r+d\). Counting only the three possible \(a\)-divisibility branches gives \((r+1)\tau(r)+\sum_{r}^{2r}\tau(n)+\sum_{r-1}^{2r-1}\tau(n)\); \(\tau(n)\le2\sqrt n\) yields the claimed bound and vanishing density. Fresh finite checks for \(2\le r\le11\) matched the quasismooth divisibility criterion against the injection condition, and for \(2\le r\le14\) matched the canonical-strip formula against direct Reid–Tai inequalities; these finite tests are supporting evidence only.

value.rationale: Quasismoothness is the central existence condition for weighted anticanonical sections, and this family has a natural two-parameter canonical region of quadratic size. Collapsing the general injection criterion to two explicit divisibility tests gives a usable complete classification, while the density-zero theorem shows a genuine asymptotic sparsity phenomenon. The result is structurally motivated and not a recomputation of a known finite list.
residual_risks: The asymptotic estimate is an upper bound sufficient for density zero; no sharp asymptotic constant for \(Q(r)\) is claimed.

final_claim: For \(r\ge2\), \(1\le a\le b\), \(d=b-a\), and \(X=\mathbb P(1^r,a,b)\), a general anticanonical hypersurface of degree \(D=r+a+b\) is quasismooth exactly when \(a\mid r\) or \(a\mid r+d\) or \(a\mid r+d-1\), and simultaneously \(b\mid r\) or \(b\mid r-d\) or \(b\mid r-d-1\). Inside the canonical strip \(0\le d\le r\), \(1\le a\le r+d\), the number \(Q(r)\) of quasismooth pairs is at most \(2(1+2\sqrt2)(r+1)\sqrt r\), hence their proportion among the \(3r(r+1)/2\) canonical pairs tends to zero.
scientific_limitations: The density theorem gives an explicit upper bound, not an asymptotic equivalent for \(Q(r)\).
The result is specific to the two-heavy family \(\mathbb P(1^r,a,b)\).
